newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS - Shekel dispute may bring new cabinet row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Shekel dispute may bring new cabinet row.

text.p: Talks on expanding the range in which the Israeli shekel can fluctuate threatened on Tuesday to erupt into a power struggle between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor.

Meridor opposes an expansion of the bands while interest rates are high, fearing the currency will appreciate, hurting exports. He has locked horns over the issue with the central bank which is pushing for wider bands to allow the market a greater say in setting the rate. Netanyahu has not taken a clear position on the issue, but has set a goal of eventually making the shekel fully convertible in world markets.

It will be up to the prime minister to make the final decision if Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel cannot resolve their dispute. Some analysts speculate Meridor would resign if Netanyahu backed the central bank's stand.
Netanyahu met the two warring sides on Monday but a marathon all-night meeting failed to resolve the issue, fuelling uncertainty on the foreign exchange market.
The Bank of Israel intervened early in the day, buying dollars to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond its trading band, a forex dealer at Bank Hapoalim said.
Political analyst Hanan Crystal said Netanyahu might be using the economic talks to move on a government shake-up.
"He has in essence begun the great battle for the whole kitty," Crystal told Israel Radio.
Israel's media have speculated that Netanyahu intended to juggle his ministers, moving Ariel Sharon from infrastructure to the finance post.
Crystal said such a plan would leave young Likud leaders like Meridor, who might challenge Netanyahu for party leadership, outside the government circle.

Netanyahu announced after the all-night meeting that a budget cut and foreign currency reform, including increasing the amount institutional investors and companies can invest abroad, had been agreed.
But talks will continue on Tuesday afternoon in Jerusalem on the main issue outstanding -- the shekel's trading bands.
The shekel strengthened in early trading. Turnover was low and spreads were very wide, reflecting the uncertainty.
"The market doesn't know what will happen," a forex dealer at Bank Hapoalim said.
Frenkel has pushed for expanding the bands, which would give the central bank some relief from the need to constantly intervene in the currency market as the currency would find its own equilibrium.
High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band.
But Dan Propper, head of the Manufacturers Association, echoed Meridor's concerns that an appreciating exchange rate would hurt the economy.
"If the trading band is expanded, we'll see higher unemployment and I'm not sure from a social perspective we'll be able to deal with this phenomenon," he told Israel Television.
The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.
Netanyahu dismissed media speculation that Meridor would quit were the bands widened.
When asked by reporters whether Meridor would continue as finance minister, Netanyahu replied: "It is not on the agenda."
